newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Hill-Select committee jostling.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Hill-Select committee jostling.

text.p: Talks over the membership of parliament's important select committees have run into problems, with the government playing hardball over Labour attempts to corner what it considers to be its share of the committee chairs.

The committees examine legislation, scrutinise departmental spending and have the power to call ministers to give evidence. They can also launch wide-ranging enquiries of their own that have the potential to severely embarrass the government.
Under the new MMP system it is assumed they will become more independent and to some extent de-politicised. Consensus and the consideration of all points of view were the catchcries.
If the current "underground" furore about the make-up of select committees is anything to go by, the auguries are not good.

Under the old rules the government dominated and chaired the select committees (but for Regulations Review which was traditional a preserve of the Opposition). A rash of defections and the creation of the United Party midway through the 1993-96 term upset the apple cart.

Under standing orders as they were revamped in August 1996, committees have eight members unless parliament orders otherwise. Overall membership must "so far as reasonably practicable, be proportional to party membership in the House".
The problems arise because with 61 seats in the 120-seat parliament the government can only expect a bare majority on the committees overall and an absolute majority on very few.
The numbers suggest a four-four split between the government and opposition members will be the norm.

The committees themselves select their chair. There is obvious potential for gridlock and little chance for Prime Minister Jim Bolger to use chairs as jobs for the boys and girls (and smooth a few ruffled feathers among those overlooked for cabinet posts) unless deals with other parties are struck beforehand.

The key for the government may be an arrangement with free- market Act New Zealand. Insiders suggest the government is working hard on this option because Act's eight seats could provide the numbers to keep the opposition in its place and squeeze it out of the most influential chairs.

It seems the government wants to limit Labour's chairs to a couple of tokens but is facing strong opposition. The normal pre-sitting horse trading is not going smoothly. It is possible that when the House sits on February 18 the shape of some committees will need to be resolved in the House itself.

Labour is already in "non-cooperation" mode in the House after being shut out of the speaker and deputy speaker positions late last year. Without some concessions on the part of the government a similar policy in the select committees could slow down a schedule already badly delayed by the coalition-building talks.
Labour deputy leader Michael Cullen told Reuters it would be "a very long year" unless the government bends.
Ken Shirley, who is negotiating on behalf of Act New Zealand, is keeping his powder dry. He said he would not rule out a debate in February on the make-up of the committees.
"It would be very imprudent for anyone (to announce the shape of the committees) before then," Shirley told Reuters.
"Our point of view is we want to chair one."

The membership of two committees in particular seem to be causing problems: Maori Affairs and the powerful Finance and Expenditure committee. Both may have to be increased in size to accommodate expectations.

New Zealand First is looking for all of its Maori MPs to be on the Maori Affairs committee, Labour is looking for strong representation -- perhaps three -- to reflect its Maori list vote while the Alliance's Mana Motuhake has a reasonable claim to a seat. If National is to find a place for Georgina Te Heu Heu as well, the committee may have to be expanded to 11 to fit everyone in.

Shirley said he could see a case for NZ First's five constituency MPs. But he said if all Maori MPs were to be on the committee, then another party could argue all its farmers should be on the Primary Production committee.

The logjam on the Finance and Expenditure committee comes partly from its importance and partly because United's sole MP Pater Dunne is keen for a seat and Act -- probably via its finance spokesman Rodney Hide -- is a keen player.
National's Tony Ryall, the senior government member of the previous committee now former chair Max Bradford is in cabinet, is the frontrunner to chair the committee.
